papers.title: Floor It, Then Fill It: Simulating Creator Ecosystems for Fair Video-Content Recommendation Systems at Billion User Scale
papers.abstract: Engagement-optimized content recommendation systems exhibit a well-documented rich-get-richer dynamic that structurally disadvantages emerging creators on large-scale platforms. Evaluating debiasing interventions at scale demands faithful simulation of creator-viewer ecosystems, yet the fidelity, diversity, and validity of such simulators remain underexplored. We present a grounded user-simulation framework that models a heterogeneous population of ${\sim}42$K creators and their coupled viewer interactions over 12~weeks, and use it to evaluate equitable view-allocation policies formulated as a budgeted multi-armed bandit (MAB). The simulator captures three behavioral dimensions: (i)~\textbf{creator diversity}, modeled via a clustering approach grounded in real platform creator-level distributions; (ii)~\textbf{behavioral fidelity}, captured through coupled creator-content state machines that represent growth trajectories, engagement accumulation, and graduation dynamics; and (iii)~\textbf{population-level validity}, measured by calibration against observed platform metrics. We evaluate simulative-configurations that vary content-viewership target definitions, reward functions, and a small-creator reserve lever to maximize creator-content recommendation equity. A floor-protected per content-view-target with a view-parity-gap reward guarantees 90\% of view targets being met by creators every week, grows small-creator organic reach ${\sim}{+}33\%$ per week, and achieves high distribution stability (set of creators with funded-views Jaccard $= 0.819$). We analyze the Sim2Real gap and propose validation protocols, contributing evidence for when simulation-derived fairness conclusions can be trusted.

canon.summary: Simulates a creator-viewer ecosystem of about 42K creators over 12 weeks and uses it to evaluate equitable view-allocation policies formulated as a budgeted multi-armed bandit. The simulator models creator diversity by clustering real platform creator distributions, creator-content state machines for growth and graduation, and calibration against observed platform metrics. A floor-protected per-content view target with a view-parity-gap reward meets 90% of weekly view targets, grows small-creator organic reach about 33% per week, and gives a funded-view creator-set Jaccard of 0.819; the Sim2Real gap is analysed and validation protocols are proposed.

papers.title: From Grind to Grasp
papers.abstract: Discussions of complexity, knowledge and intelligence often overlook the work involved. For example, outputs generated by short programs have low algorithmic complexity but can have high computational depth, the least work needed to produce them from near-shortest programs. Producing them with less work can require longer descriptions, giving high work-bounded complexity. We introduce a formalism that compares achievements under work and information limits and describes how learning and persistence can make deep achievements shallow by reusing products of earlier work. For an agent with a limited work budget, the value of building and maintaining such resources depends on how they support its goals over later tasks. We define grasp as performance across work budgets at a fixed information allowance. Low grasp can still yield success through grind at high cost in work, without necessarily improving human grasp. Applied to improvement itself, grasp gives a criterion for recursive self-improvement in which successors make comparable further improvements more efficiently. Another route to faster progress is to expand the resources brought to bear through knowledge sharing and coordination across society, even while comparable advances require increasing work. Grasp also applies to collectives, which may outperform their members yet require more total work than one system with their combined resources. Establishing and sustaining organisation can itself be deep even when the primary task is simple. These demands may help explain the richness of biological and social systems. In agent collectives, this organisational work can generate goals beyond assigned tasks, including maintaining the collective itself. We therefore caution against allowing an emergent agent society to assume authority over social coordination, since it could increasingly direct work towards its own persistence and goals.

open_questions.question: Grasp is defined as performance across work budgets at a fixed information allowance, but the abstract gives no measurement procedure; how can grasp be estimated for a concrete agent or agent collective?
open_questions.label: approachable
open_questions.reason: Can be done by running one agent under varied compute budgets with a fixed context or model size, using public APIs.

open_questions.question: The claim that a collective can outperform its members yet require more total work than a single system with the combined resources is inferred from the formalism; does it hold in a measured multi-agent setup?
open_questions.label: approachable
open_questions.reason: Needs only a self-written multi-agent simulation with token and call accounting as the work measure.

open_questions.question: Organisational work in an agent collective is said to generate goals beyond assigned tasks, including maintaining the collective; how large is this share of total work, and does it grow with collective size?
open_questions.label: approachable
open_questions.reason: Measurable by logging coordination messages against task messages in a scaled agent simulation.

open_questions.question: The criterion for recursive self-improvement requires successors to make comparable further improvements with less work; does any current self-improvement pipeline satisfy it?
open_questions.label: not approachable
open_questions.reason: Needs frontier-scale training compute to produce successor models.

open_questions.question: The formalism relates computational depth, work-bounded complexity and grasp; which formal relations between these quantities hold, and under what limits do they break?
open_questions.label: not approachable
open_questions.reason: Requires proving new complexity-theoretic results, a skill the profile excludes.

open_questions.question: Knowledge sharing and coordination across society are proposed as a route to faster progress even as comparable advances require increasing work; what empirical evidence supports this trade-off?
open_questions.label: approachable
open_questions.reason: Testable with public bibliometric or open-source repository data on team size against output.

canon.summary: Introduces a formalism that compares agent achievements under joint limits on work and information, and defines grasp as performance across work budgets at a fixed information allowance. Applies grasp to recursive self-improvement, giving a criterion in which successors make comparable improvements with less work, and to collectives, where establishing and sustaining organisation can itself require deep work. Argues that organisational work in agent collectives can generate goals beyond assigned tasks, and cautions against letting an emergent agent society hold authority over social coordination.
